title: A Nearly Quartic Separation Between Randomized and Quantum Query Complexity
main_claim: Total functions F_{k,m} with Q ≤ √m·polylog and R ≥ m^{2-1/k}/log²m, so the optimal exponent in R(f)=O(Q(f)^α) is 4 (disproving the ABKRT cubic conjecture).

issues.description: The paper says BS21 applies to exactly the thresholds δ=2^{-5k} (yes case) and δ/2 (no case). I could not check BS21's exact thresholds offline. A mismatch would not matter: the quantum algorithm, the exact circuit and the lower-bound use all work for any constant gap, and changing the gap only affects constants and log factors.
issues.evidence: The integer comparisons 2^{5k}N ≥ M and 2^{5k+1}|N| ≤ M, with M=m·√m^{k-1}, were checked. The quantum algorithm separates success probability Φ² ≥ δ² from Φ² ≤ δ²/4.

coverage: Read everything: the construction, Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2, the bounded-amplification lemma (checked the Grover average bound of at least 9/20 and the trial-failure rate of 31/40), the tournament proposition (checked the drift identity E[W_new]=(W²−Σw_i²)/(2W) using a_ij+a_ji=1, the bound (1−ε)^T>1/2, Markov, and the coupling with sampler failures), the column comparison (a winner beats any opponent with probability at least 1−ε even when the opponent's input is outside the promise, because no pointer can hit a zero in an all-ones X), the verification step and the error accounting, and the classical lower bound (coupling of dummy and planted inputs, zero-finding E Z ≤ 4G/m, the heavy-column bound, the simulator plus the capped adaptive direct product, which is the standard Drucker/Shaltiel supermartingale argument, minimax giving β ≤ 2/3, and G(2/3)^r = o(1) with r = 20 log m). The exponent derivation is fine. The appendix (ABKRT D=O(Q⁴)) was skimmed. Consistency check: D ≤ C1·bs ≤ (m·polylog)(m·polylog) = m²·polylog, which is compatible with the m^{2−1/k} lower bound.
